tier_reason: Upgraded from B: the fast-sp repo (a third-party demo, not a well-known suite, so B does not fit) publishes the benchmark code (src/lib.rs #[bench] harness, src/implementations/rust_portable_simd.rs, rust_for_loop.rs, rust_iter.rs, c/*.c, build.rs) running portable_simd against scalar Rust and C loops. The README states rustc 1.68.0-nightly (2023-01-12) / LLVM 15.0.6, Apple clang 14.0.0 and the Apple M1 CPU, and the flags follow from the public build files: the default cargo bench profile, and cc with -mcpu=apple-m1 in build.rs.

corrections.workload: Independent 'sp' benchmark from the 'six times faster than C' blog post: return the number of 's' bytes minus the number of 'p' bytes over 12 MiB of random 's'/'p' characters (random_sp) or 12 MiB of random printable ASCII (random_printable). The Rust portable_simd version compares 16 bytes at a time (u8x16) against scalar Rust (for-loop, iterator), C (original, while-loop, for-loop) and NumPy versions.
corrections.claimed_speedup: random_sp: portable_simd 19.874 GiB/s (589,654 ns/iter) vs Rust iter 3.978 GiB/s, Rust for_loop 1.482 GiB/s, C for_loop 1.482 GiB/s, C original 0.278 GiB/s, NumPy 5.711 GiB/s; about 5.0x over the Rust iterator and 13.4x over the Rust and C for-loops (derived from page data). random_printable: 19.870 vs 3.979 (Rust iter), 1.481 (Rust for_loop) and 1.478 GiB/s (C for_loop and C original).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.68.0-nightly (61a415be5 2023-01-12), LLVM 15.0.6; Apple clang 14.0.0 (clang-1400.0.29.202) for the C rows. Run with cargo bench. Cargo.toml has no profile overrides, so the default bench profile applies (opt-level 3, no target-cpu flag). build.rs compiles the C sources through the cc crate with -mcpu=apple-m1 and the optimization level of the cargo profile.
corrections.caveats: The measured repo (eddieantonio/fast-sp) is a third-party, single-author demo with 3 stars and AGPL-3.0 benchmark code; the library itself is Apache-2.0 OR MIT. It covers one microbenchmark (count of 's' minus count of 'p') on one Apple M1 machine (NEON, 16-byte vectors) with a 2023-01-12 nightly, so today's portable_simd may differ. The README table comes from the 2023 code. On 2026-07-30 the author moved rust_portable_simd.rs to std::simd::prelude and added a rust_portable_simd_v2 variant, but did not re-run the table. The baselines are scalar loops for the same task. The README says the Rust and C for-loops compile to branchless scalar code (cinc/csel) and the iterator version autovectorizes into messy code, so the win is explicit SIMD over scalar or weakly autovectorized code, not over another SIMD library. No comparison against std::arch intrinsics, C++ std::experimental::simd, xsimd or Highway was found. The portable-simd README has no benchmark numbers, and the book's roughly 41 percent matrix-multiply figure (first-party, measured on the author's machine) was not checked. Correctness is tested in the repo: all implementations are asserted equal on both 12 MiB inputs. Timing uses Rust's built-in nightly #[bench] harness with the input behind black_box. Portable-simd PR #548 (AVX2 swizzle_dyn) reports 33 percent less time on a 'Zen2 laptop', but it measures against the library's own previous code and states no CPU model, compiler or benchmark code.

notes: Numbers match the fast-sp README exactly. The record's workload wrongly said 'count transitions'; it is a net count. Tier A rests on flags read from the public Cargo.toml and build.rs rather than stated in prose; B was wrong either way, because this is neither a paper nor a well-known suite. Metadata checked on github.com (gh CLI blocked): 1.1k stars, Apache-2.0 and MIT, not archived, last commit 2026-09-16 on main.

tier_reason: First-party numbers in the README and the per-example readmes. The benchmark code (examples/*/benchmark.sh, hyperfine, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native') is public, and two of the three CPU models are named, but the rustc nightly and ISPC versions are not stated, so the evidence falls short of A. The tier stays C; the claim and caveats were overstated and are corrected.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README summary, packed_simd+rayon vs ISPC: aobench [-1.02x, +1.53x]; stencil [+1.06x, +1.72x]; mandelbrot [-1.74x, +1.2x]; options_pricing black_scholes +1.0x, binomial_put +1.4x ('+' is speed-up, '-' slowdown). Per-example readmes, parallel Rust vs ISPC with tasks: aobench tiled_par 98 ms vs ispc_tasks 150 ms on the 28-core Xeon E5-2690 v4, 102 vs 153 ms on the 40-core Xeon Gold 6148, 578 vs 567 ms on the dual-core i5. Stencil: vector_par 444 vs ispc_tasks 470 ms on the i5. On the E5-2690 v4, vector_par 167 ms vs serial ispc 287 ms and ispc_tasks 395 ms; the readme's '1.72x faster than ispc_tasks' equals 287/167 (the serial ispc row), while against ispc_tasks it is 2.37x (derived from page data). On the Gold 6148, 148 vs serial ispc 185 ms (1.25x). Mandelbrot, parallel simd vs ispc (ISPC with tasks): 21.0 vs 25.7 ms on the i5, 25.1 vs 14.4 ms on the E5-2690 v4 (1.74x slower), 29.9 vs 30.3 ms on the Gold 6148. Options_pricing, i5 only: Black-Scholes par_simd 246 vs ispc+tasks 248 ms; binomial put par_simd 279 vs ispc+tasks 404 ms. Single-thread packed_simd vs serial ISPC: aobench tiled 1328 vs 1158 ms (i5), 640 vs 576 ms (E5) and 770 vs 491 ms (Gold), so ISPC wins on all three; stencil vector 630 vs 558 ms (i5), 276 vs 287 ms (E5), 278 vs 185 ms (Gold); Black-Scholes simd 367 vs 360 ms, binomial put simd 651 vs 805 ms (i5). Single-thread SIMD vs the crate's own scalar loop on the i5: aobench vector 4.0x (1458 vs 5884 ms), stencil vector 4.5x (630 vs 2842 ms). Mandelbrot's 4.1x (21.0 vs 86.6 ms) is the parallel simd algorithm on two cores, not single-thread.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc nightly (the rust-toolchain file says only 'nightly', with no pinned date). examples/*/benchmark.sh builds with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release --no-default-features and times each algorithm with hyperfine. The aobench script builds and times both a 256bit-feature and a 128-bit build, and the readme does not say which one the table shows. ISPC is built through the ispc crate, and examples/aobench/build.rs targets the SSE2, SSE4, AVX1, AVX2 and AVX512KNL ISAs. The rustc and ispc versions and the ISPC optimization flags are not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from the project's own examples. The README ranges mix wins and losses: aobench and mandelbrot each have a slowdown, and mandelbrot on the 28-core Xeon is 1.74x slower than ISPC. The headline wins come from rayon-parallel Rust variants against ISPC task builds. Single-threaded, packed_simd mostly matches or trails serial ISPC: aobench serial ISPC is faster on all three machines (up to 770 vs 491 ms on the Gold 6148), and stencil serial ISPC is faster on the i5 and the Gold 6148. So the wins measure rayon's thread scaling more than SIMD code generation. The ISPC task baseline looks crippled on the many-core Xeons: stencil ispc_tasks is slower than serial ispc (395 vs 287 ms on the E5-2690 v4, 401 vs 185 ms on the Gold 6148). The stencil readme labels its E5-2690 v4 ratio of 1.72x as 'vs ispc_tasks', but the ratio matches the serial ispc row. In the binomial put table the speedup column does not match the times (ispc 805 ms is listed as 7.4x and par_simd 279 ms as 4.3x against the 2057 ms scalar run), so use the time column. Mandelbrot 'simd' is a parallel algorithm and mandelbrot 'ispc' uses ISPC tasks; on the Xeons both reach only about 2x over scalar for 14-30 ms runs. Hyperfine times the whole process, so process start and thread-pool setup are inside the timed region. The results are undated (the examples date from about 2018), the rustc nightly and ISPC versions are not stated, and the i5 model is not given, so the runs are not fully reproducible. The baseline is ISPC, not std::arch or platform intrinsics, and no direct intrinsics comparison was found. The repository was archived (read-only) on 2026-09-16. The last code change was 2023-07-30 (0.3.9), the 2026-09-15 commit is the deprecation notice, and the crate is superseded by rust-lang/portable-simd (std::simd). The book's claim about this crate was not consulted.

notes: All quoted numbers appear in the example readmes. The verdict is downgrade because the claim and caveats overstated the result, not because the tier changed. The record said the serial ISPC rows are slower, but serial ISPC beats serial packed_simd on aobench on every machine. It also called the mandelbrot 4.1x single-thread, but that algorithm is parallel. Metadata checked on github.com: 649 stars, Apache-2.0 and MIT, archived 2026-09-16, last commit 2026-09-15; maintenance_status 'abandoned' is correct.
